title: Function Templates
summary: A **template** is a pattern for a function with a placeholder type `T`. The compiler generates a real function for each type you use it with. Write it once and it works for `int`, `double`, `std::string` and more.
markdown:
## The problem: the same code for every type Overloading lets these share a name, but you still write each body: ```cpp int maxOf(int a, int b) { return a > b ? a : b; } double maxOf(double a, double b) { return a > b ? a : b; } // ...and again for every other type ``` The bodies are identical. Only the type changes. A **function template** lets you write the body once and leave the type as a parameter. ```cpp #include #include template T maxOf(T a, T b) { return a > b ? a : b; } int main() { std::cout << maxOf(3, 7) << '\n'; // T is int std::cout << maxOf(2.5, 1.5) << '\n'; // T is double std::cout << maxOf('a', 'z') << '\n'; // T given explicitly return 0; } ``` `template ` introduces `T` as a **type parameter**: a stand-in for a type that is filled in later. ## Instantiation A template is not a function. It is a recipe from which the compiler makes functions on demand. ```mermaid flowchart TD T["template <typename T>
T maxOf(T a, T b)"] -->|"maxOf(3, 7)"| I["int maxOf(int, int)"] T -->|"maxOf(2.5, 1.5)"| D["double maxOf(double, double)"] T -->|"maxOf(s1, s2)"| S["std::string maxOf(std::string, std::string)"] ``` Generating a concrete function from a template is called **instantiation**. It happens at compile time, once per distinct type, and the result is exactly as fast as a function written by hand. ## Deducing `T` Usually you do not say what `T` is. The compiler works it out from the arguments, which is called **template argument deduction**. | Call | Result | |---|---| | `maxOf(3, 7)` | Both are `int`, so `T` is `int` | | `maxOf(3, 7.5)` | Error: `T` cannot be both `int` and `double` | | `maxOf(3, 7.5)` | You chose `T`; the `3` is converted to `3.0` | Deduction does not apply conversions. Each argument must agree on `T` exactly. ### More than one type parameter When the arguments may legitimately have different types, give each its own parameter: ```cpp template auto addMixed(T a, U b) { return a + b; } addMixed(3, 7.5); // T is int, U is double, the result is double ``` `auto` as the return type asks the compiler to work it out from the `return` statement. ### The short form Since C++20, `auto` in a parameter list makes a function a template without the `template` line: ```cpp auto addMixed(auto a, auto b) { return a + b; } ``` Each `auto` parameter is its own independent type parameter. ## The type has to support what the body does A template compiles for a given type only if every operation in its body is valid for that type. ```cpp struct Cat {}; maxOf(Cat{}, Cat{}); // error: Cat has no operator> ``` The error is reported at the point of instantiation, and for templates it can be long. C++20 **concepts** let a template state its requirements up front, which gives far clearer errors: [[9.04 Concepts (C++20)]]. ## Templates live in headers To instantiate a template, the compiler must see its full body at the place where it is used. A declaration alone is not enough. | Kind of function | Declaration | Definition | |---|---|---| | Ordinary | Header | `.cpp` file | | Template | Header | **Header as well** | ## Check yourself ```quiz ? When is a function actually generated from a template? - When the program starts running - When the template is first written in the header + At compile time, when the template is used with a specific type - Once per call, while the program runs > Using the template with a type makes the compiler generate (instantiate) that version during the build. ? Why does `maxOf(3, 4.5)` fail? - Templates cannot work with `double` + `T` would have to be both `int` and `double` - `maxOf` needs at least three arguments - The compiler converts both to `int` and loses the `.5` > Deduction finds `int` from one argument and `double` from the other, so it fails. Write `maxOf(3, 4.5)` or use two type parameters. ? Why must a template's body be in the header? - Because templates cannot be declared without a body - Because the linker refuses to link `.cpp` files with templates - Because headers compile faster than `.cpp` files + The compiler needs the full body to generate code for each type > To instantiate a template for a type, the compiler must see its full definition in that file, so it goes in the header. ? What happens if you use a template with a type that lacks a required operation? - The function silently does nothing for that type - The program crashes when that line runs + A compile error at the point of instantiation - The compiler converts the value to `int` first > The generated function would contain invalid code, such as `<` on a type that has none, so the build fails. ```
ideas:
1. Write the templates `minOf`, `clampValue(T value, T low, T high)` and `printTwice(T x)`.
2. Call `maxOf(std::string{ "apple" }, std::string{ "banana" })`. Which wins, and why?
3. Write `template <typename T> T sumTo(T n)` that adds 1 up to n. Call it with an `int` and a `long long`.

cards.q: When is a function actually generated from a template?
cards.a:
At compile time, when the template is used with a specific type

Using the template with a type makes the compiler generate (instantiate) that version during the build.

`T` would have to be both `int` and `double`

Deduction finds `int` from one argument and `double` from the other, so it fails. Write `maxOf<double>(3, 4.5)` or use two type parameters.

cards.q: Why must a template's body be in the header?
cards.a:
The compiler needs the full body to generate code for each type

To instantiate a template for a type, the compiler must see its full definition in that file, so it goes in the header.

cards.q: What happens if you use a template with a type that lacks a required operation?
cards.a:
A compile error at the point of instantiation

The generated function would contain invalid code, such as `<` on a type that has none, so the build fails.
